content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper addresses the issue with representing (esp. heterophilic, power law) graphs by factorising the adjacency matrix into a combination of homophilic and heterophilic factors that are interpretable. Lower bounds based on logisitic principal components analysis (LPCA) is improved removing assumptions on the max degree and replacing with the arboricity of the graph. A new graph model is proposed with symmetric and non-negative factorisations based on the decomposition mentioned and a simple gradient descent alogirthm is proposed to optimise the paramters. The method is compared to a baseline SVD decomposition and recent work using a similar method, BigClam. Results on synthetic and real-world data are reported with promising results.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
This paper addresses the issue of modelling graphs with both homophily and heterophily in a elegent decomposition that is both simple and effective. The new lower bound is novel and seems valid to the best of my knowledge but I could not follow all steps in detail due to time constraints and lack of deep knowledge in the area. The algorithm to optimise the model is simple and results looked promising. This is very relevant work, and a hot topic in graph related domains including GNNs for example.

I do wonder about the comparison with the other methods, as in the comparison with synthetic data, the BigClam method was limited to 12 factors, when I think using 20 factors would be interesting, and may lead to improved fitting of the BiClam method. With the synthetic data, the exact number of homophilic factors was known (10 towns) and number of heterophilic were known (2 genders), leading to an over simplified problem, as this knoweldge is unknown for a real problem. Some more details about how many features and other parameter tuning of the comparison models in the results would also be important to understand if these seem optimal.

content.title: Response to Reviewer s4Ez Part 1
content.comment:
Thank you for the extensive review. We address the questions and concerns piecewise:

**Q1**: Fig. 1 - can you add some details on the sampling?

**Response**: As suggested, we have now included some clarifying text in the caption of Figure 1 to make it more clear and understandable. The “Expected Adjacency” on the left is a matrix of probabilities that edges appear, with entries in $[0,1]$. The “Sampled Adjacency” on the right is a binary matrix, with entries in $\\{0,1\\}$, for an unweighted graph which was sampled based on that matrix. In particular, letting $\tilde{\boldsymbol{A}}$ be the former matrix and $\boldsymbol{A}$ be the latter one, for $i \leq j$, we have $\boldsymbol{A}\_{ij} \sim \textrm{Bernoulli} (\tilde{\boldsymbol{A}}\_{ij}) $. 

**Q2**: Could you elaborate on why kB + kC = 6k is required?

**Response**: Given the logits of a rank-$k$ factorization of a graph in the LPCA model, that is, the $\boldsymbol{X} \boldsymbol{Y}^\top$, we first symmetrize the logits, i.e., we use the mean of $\boldsymbol{X} \boldsymbol{Y}^\top$ and $\boldsymbol{Y} \boldsymbol{X}^\top$. Note that increases the rank of the factorization by a factor of at most $2$, up to $2k$. We then must convert the factorization with unconstrained $\boldsymbol{X}, \boldsymbol{Y}^\top$ into one with nonnegative factors. As shown in Lemma 4.3, this can increase the rank of the factorization by a factor of at most $3$, up to $6k$. We have added some clarifying text outlining the preceding right after Equation 5 where $k_B + k_C = 6k$ is stated.
Also, please note that this is only for the theoretical results with our proposed nonnegative symmetric factorization.

**Q3**: If I understand correctly, homophilic clusters, in B, are found as those with positive eigenvalues and heterophilic clusters, in C, those with negative eigenvalues?

**Response**: Exactly. And this is the salient difference between our work and, e.g., BigClam, which does not include some equivalent of $\boldsymbol{C}$.

**Q4**: How to choose the kB and kC parameter values? Can these eigenvalues above somehow help with this, although for large data this probably not computationally feasible, can you comment?

**Response**: It may be possible to automatically select a $k_B/k_C$ split by using Algorithm 1 (note that this algorithm does not require $k_B,k_C$ as input), then discarding columns of the factorization with least contribution, e.g., to the Frobenius norm of the matrix.
However, we find that it generally does not make much of a difference on real-world graphs relative to a half/half split. Related to your suggestion, this may be reflected in the fact that large real-world networks tend to have a roughly equal number of extremal negative and positive eigenvalues.

If you are referring to selecting the total number of clusters $k_B+k_C$, this is likely best set based on the application (e.g., as a hyperparameter set by cross-validation), though it may be possible to also set within our framework with a heuristic like, e.g., the elbow method, based on the drop in Frobenius error as embedding dimensionality is increased.

content.title: Response to Reviewer s4Ez Part 2
content.comment:
**Q5**: Add reference to “Community Detection in Attributed Graphs: An Embedding Approach”

**Response**: Thank you for the suggested reference, which we have integrated into the paper. As you note, this work focuses on a model which assumes homophily, in contrast to ours.

**Q6**: In Figure 3 the learnt features are shown, and the proposed method has captured the ten cities and the additional 2 gender features. Big Clam only learns the ten cities; have you tried with 20 features and BigClam, as this has the potential to learn each combination of GENDER X CITY as an independent feature element?... if the other methods, like BigClam have more features, like 20 in the synthetic example, are they able to learn as well given the extra capacity?

**Response**: This is a great question. First, we note that BigClam indeed fails to represent the synthetic graph even with a 20-dimensional embedding: we run this experiment and plot the result in Figure 2 (right). Regarding your specific idea of what would happen if BigClam learned each combination of Gender x City as a separate feature, say, in a binary feature matrix $\boldsymbol{B} \in \\{0,1\\}^{n \times 20}$: When you calculate $\boldsymbol{B} \boldsymbol{B}^\top$, you will notice that it comprises several blocks along the diagonal, corresponding to people in the same Gender x City group being linked. The heterophilous behavior of gender in this example, which involves the dominance of off-diagonal entries, necessitates a non-positive semidefinite factorization.

That being said, SVD is indeed capable of fitting the graph with 20 features, but not 12 like our model. The presence of the sigmoid nonlinearity in our model makes it combinatorially more powerful than SVD, which has no nonlinearity. In the motivating example, our method requires 2+10=12 dimensions to capture the graph structure, compared to 2\*10=20 for SVD, which indeed is not a large difference. But the difference would be much larger with additional latent variables beyond 2 genders and 10 cities (e.g., 2+10+5+8 vs 2\*10\*5\*8).


It is these limitations that motivate this work, which is broadly about the benefits and considerations when simultaneously incorporating nonnegativity, heterophily (i.e., no PSD assumption), and nonlinearity into a graph factorization.

**Q7**: Adding file versions as text in the README or a requirements.txt can solve this problem, including the Python version.

**Response**: This is a good suggestion – we will add this information in the final version.

**Q8**: I would reconsider the example of only heterogeneous dating sites… How about an example with fraudsters and customers like in this review [Zheng et al. 2022]? Could it even be enough to just say that in a same-gender dating site the example would actually be homophilic between genders so we use a hetersexual example?

**Response**: Thank you for the thoughtful suggestion. We have added the suggested note about how a mostly homosexual dating app would not exhibit heterophily in this sense. If the ethics review suggests further changes, we will change to the fraudsters/customers example from Zheng et al. – thank you for this reference.

---

Peysakhovich, Alexander, and Leon Bottou. "An attract-repel decomposition of undirected networks." arXiv preprint arXiv:2106.09671 (2021).

content.title: Response to Post Reviewer-Discussion Update
content.comment:
Thank you for explaining your reasoning for lowering your score. 

> the similarity to the work on Generalized RDPG was brought up and this area of work is not compared in enough detail considering the similarity with the work on homopholic and heterophilic relations

As we have stated elsewhere, this work is broadly about the benefits and considerations when simultaneously incorporating nonnegativity, heterophily / non-PSDness, and nonlinearity into a graph factorization. Our work lies at the intersection of these three aspects, but there is a lot of prior work that touches on one or two of them. We are currently citing around 40 works in the related work section, so in the interest of space, we discuss them to varying extents, hoping to paint a concise but holistic picture of prior factorization-based models and how they relate to ours. The means of incorporating heterophily in GRDPG is somewhat related to those in Peysakhovich & Bottou (2021), Miller et al. (2009), and, to a lesser extent, Nourbakhsh et al. (2014). In particular, we believe the overlap between our work and that of Peysakhovich & Bottou, which also discusses heterophily quite extensively, largely encompasses the overlap between our work and the GRDPG paper, which is why we discuss the former in more detail. All of these works allow for heterophily by letting the factorization be non-PSD in some way, so we group their discussion together. (More specifically, the $\boldsymbol{B} \boldsymbol{B}^\top - \boldsymbol{C} \boldsymbol{C}^\top$ and $\boldsymbol{V} \boldsymbol{W} \boldsymbol{V}^\top$ sort of factorizations are essentially equivalent to GRDPG's $\boldsymbol{X} \boldsymbol{I}_{p,q} \boldsymbol{X}^\top$ up to some simple algebraic manipulations, at least in the absence of nonnegativity constraints.)\
To be clear, like the authors of the GRDPG paper, we are not claiming objective superiority of our factorization, and the amount of discussion of each prior method reflects a holistic relevance to our focuses rather than some such objective ranking. Specifically, in this work, a major focus is low-rank expressiveness guarantees. For our arboricity-based bound (as well as prior bounds based on max-degree), it is essential to have a nonlinearity, which is not present in GRDPG, hence the briefer discussion of that work. Also, on the empirical side, as we note in the response to Reviewer pv1p, SVD is the closest that any nonlinearity-less low-rank factorization can approximate an adjacency matrix (in terms of Frobenius error), and we find that our model can be fit to be significantly closer than this in experiments on real-world graphs. (On the other hand, the lack of a nonlinearity in GRDPG facilitates interesting convergence guarantees related to spectral theory.) Note also that neither the GRDPG paper nor that of Peysakhovich & Bottou discuss nonnegativity of the factors, hence the focus elsewhere on BigClam, which does discuss nonnegativity. We would add to the final related works section some more discussion of any specifics (discussed above or otherwise) that reviewers believe are important, though we would have to be selective in the main paper due to space constraints.

> There was also some questions about the bound, to be clarified.

> ensuring that the real-data experiments are strongly supporting the claims (datasets are those which have heterophilic and homophilic relations, and the comparable methods are state-of-the-art)

We are happy to answer any questions about the bound. If the questions relate to Reviewer N53t's comments about tightness of the arboricity bound in practice, perhaps some of them have been addressed in that response. Similarly, in that response, we have tried to address broad concerns about empirical evaluation which were raised by the same reviewer, and we are happy to take further questions. As before, we note that we primarily emphasize the conceptual/theoretical contributions of this work rather than empirical ones.

---

Nourbakhsh, Farshad, Samuel Rota Bulo, and Marcello Pelillo. "A matrix factorization approach to graph compression." 22nd International Conference on Pattern Recognition. IEEE, 2014.

Miller, Kurt, Michael Jordan, and Thomas Griffiths. "Nonparametric latent feature models for link prediction." NeurIPS, 2009.

Peysakhovich, Alexander, and Leon Bottou. "An attract-repel decomposition of undirected networks." arXiv preprint arXiv:2106.09671 (2021).

content.summary_of_the_paper:
In this paper, the authors propose a representation model in the framework of describing an adjacency matrix through matrix factorization. They also prove a result regarding exact matrix representation, where the needed size of the embeddings can be described in terms of the arboricity of the graph. This improves previous results in terms of applicability to real graphs.
Finally, the authors propose an alternative learning method for the factorization based on gradient descent, which is then used for downstream tasks in the experimental section.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The strength of the paper is the result regarding arboricity and the factorization of the adjacency matrix.

However, I find a significant weakness. There is a quite big community working in graph models via factorization, or "dot product graphs", which is not acknowledged in the paper. I'm sure this is not intentional, but the amount of work of these groups is quite large, and published in journals and conferences very related to this one (meaning that this is not a case of similar work but in a very different community) like NeurIPS or PAMI.
Namely, the RDPG model is widely studied and not mentioned in the paper. The model is almost exactly like the ones described in this work, and moreover, there is a version called Generalized RDPG which takes into account heterophily and homophily, and its formulation is very related to the one proposed in this paper (in equation 3).

I think the Generalized RDPG model is described in this paper:
P. Rubin-Delanchy, J. Cape, M. Tang, and C. E. Priebe, "A statistical interpretation of spectral embedding: The generalized random dot product graph," 2017

and some other papers on the subject are:
 - E. Scheinerman and K. Tucker, "Modeling graphs using dot product representations," Comput. Stat.
 - A. Athreya, D. E. Fishkind, M. Tang, C. E. Priebe, Y. Park, J. T.
Vogelstein, K. Levin, V. Lyzinski, and Y. Qin, "Statistical inference on random dot product graphs: A survey,"
 - I. Gallagher, A. Jones, and P. Rubin-Delanchy, "Spectral embedding
for dynamic networks with stability guarantees," Advances in Neural
Information Processing Systems 34, NeurIPS, 2021.
 - B. Marenco et. al, Online change-point detection for weighted and directed random dot product graphs. IEEE Transactions on Signal and Information Processing over Networks, 2022.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is well written in general, the results are clearly stated (and the proof is easy to follow). As far as I know, this result (regarding arboricity) is original and is an interesting extension of existing work. However, the formulation of the model is very related to existing work, which is not described in the paper (see previous section).

The code is included as supplementary material, so this is a good point too.

I'm sure the authors will take into account these (and maybe other) related papers and will come up with a new version, which would be a very nice paper.

content.title: Response to Reviewer pv1p
content.comment:
Thank you for the suggestions. We have carefully addressed your comments in the updated paper.

**Q1**: Missing references to random dot product models

**Response**: Thanks for pointing out these related papers. We have now included references to these papers in the revised draft, and included another relevant one (Nourbaksh et al. 2014) that we found as well.

**Q2**: Discuss relation of model to Generalized RDPG and other dot product models

**Response**: Thanks for this suggestion. We have added a mention of the Generalized RDPG model and positioned it relative to the others we discuss in the updated draft. The GRDPG is an interesting approach to integrating heterophily into these models. We note that the RDPG models do not have a nonlinear linking function (e.g, $\sigma$, the logistic function as in our model), which is crucial to our representation results. This includes both the theoretical exact representation guarantees, as well as the empirical error minimization results in Figure 4, given that SVD lower bounds Frobenius approximation error for all rank-$k$ factorizations without a nonlinearity, including RDPG and GRDPG. In this regard, the model of Miller et al. (2009) is closer to ours, which we have also discussed in paper. Broadly, this work is about the benefits and considerations when simultaneously incorporating nonnegativity, heterophily (i.e., no PSD assumption), and nonlinearity into a graph factorization, so while a lot of prior work touches on one or two aspects, there is fairly little at the intersection of all three.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes an exact nonnegative matrix factorization method that provides interpretable node embeddings (interpretation as the cluster/community assignment). The authors prove that under the constraint of embedding dimensionality, the embeddings can reconstruct adjacency matrix exactly. A training algorithm is provided and shown to be effective in community detection and interpretable link prediction.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The proposed model is interpretable to provide node embeddings that can be interpreted as cluster assignments.
- The paper theoretically proves under certain embedding dimensionality, the node embeddings can be used to perfectly reconstruct the input adjacency matrix.
- The graph model can explicitly capture the homophily and heterophily of the graph.
- An illustrative example is provided in the introduction to help understand the motivations of this work.

Weaknesses:
- It's not clear whether the embedding dimension condition on arboricit is tighter than the existing degree-based theorem.
- The proposed algorithm has a high complexity given that it computes the reconstructed dense adjacency matrix in each iteration (BB^T-CC^T).
- Interpretable link prediction is not a new application, but in the experiments only few methods are compared. 
- The heterophily of the datasets is not clearly justified.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The novelty is good since it studies the exactness of the embeddings on graphs with both homophily and heterophily.
The paper overall is clear and not hard to follow.
It's not clear whether the results presented in the paper is implemented based on the stochastic version or non-stochastic version.
content.summary_of_the_review:
To further justify the weaknesses:
- It's not clear whether 4 * \alpha^2 is a smaller number than 2c (where c is the max degree). In appendix, the authors provide the value of degeneracy, but based on that number, 4 * \alpha^2 is definitely much larger than 2c. In this way, I don't think the bound based on arboricit has a wider applicability.  
- Regarding the heterophily of the datasets, though the authors illustrate the heterophily intuitively, it's not quantified. Thus, it's unable to justify whether the proposed method can model heterophily in practice.

content.title: Response to Reviewer N53t
content.comment:
Thanks for your comments. We address the comments, which fall into two categories:

**Q1**: Applicability to real-world datasets

**Response**: First, we note that this work is primarily conceptual. Broadly, it is about the benefits and considerations when simultaneously incorporating nonnegativity, heterophily (i.e., no PSD assumption), and nonlinearity into a graph factorization. There is a line of work on limitations of factorization-based models for representing graphs, and we mainly intend our work to advance conceptual/theoretical understanding in this area. The empirical section is simply meant to suggest that capturing heterophily can be beneficial for factorizations in downstream tasks. As an aside, this is why we only compare to factorization-based methods for interpretable link prediction. The stochastic version of the training algorithm is noted mainly as a contrast to some other prior algorithms, which do not admit a scalable version - we employ the non-stochastic version for the empirical results in this work. Relatedly, we work with small to medium sized datasets, which may be why the arboricity/degeneracy bound seems insignificant. Degeneracy can be far more tractable for large real-world networks, see, e.g., Table 2 in Noujan et al. (2021). We also reiterate that degeneracy, though it can be computed relatively easily, is only an upper bound on arboricity, and degeneracy is an upper bound on max degree.

**Q2**: Can you quantify heterophily in real-world datasets?

**Response**: Apologies for the confusion. To our knowledge, there is no well-accepted quantitative definition of heterophily that is applicable to these experiments. There is a definition in some prior work (see GeomGCN below) that has seen popularity in related papers: it defines heterophily in terms of ground-truth class/label data (i.e., what fraction of edges are between nodes of the same class), but this is not applicable to our setting of overlapping communities and multiple labels per node. As our illustrative example suggests, it may be possible to naturally define heterophily without reference to ground-truth labels. In fact, we hope that this work can serve as a basis for such definition of heterophily, since there is a significant difference between how well our model and BigClam, the salient distinction between which is the inclusion of a heterophilous term in the factorization, can match a given adjacency matrix (as in our Figure 4).

As you note, aside from the preceding, we do include a fairly concrete and very intuitive synthetic demonstration of modeling heterophily in Figures 1-3, and we discuss heterophilous aspects of some of the real-world datasets in Appendix A.2. Beyond matching the adjacency matrix, incorporating a heterophilous term also seems to improve the ability to predict links and ground truth communities (Figure 5).

---

Pashanasangi, Noujan, and C. Seshadhri. "Faster and generalized temporal triangle counting, via degeneracy ordering." KDD, 2021.

Pei, Hongbin, Bingzhe Wei, Kevin Chen-Chuan Chang, Yu Lei, and Bo Yang. "Geom-GCN: Geometric Graph Convolutional Networks." ICLR, 2019.

content.title: Post-review discussion
content.comment: Thank you for clarifying and addressing the concerns in my review. I agree that this work is more conceptual than practical especially along the direction of factorization-based embedding methods. Despite this, I have a follow-up question: how does it perform when you use the stochastic version?

content.title: Response to Follow-up
content.comment: Thank you for following up. Yes, we primarily emphasize the conceptual/theoretical contribution of this work as opposed to the empirical. To respond to your question, in some informal experiments on stochastic versions of each of the factorization-based algorithms, we generally found that they all see some reduction in performance in terms of reconstruction error, but still our method generally achieves the closest fit. In other words, we find that the greater theoretical capabilities of our model to fit graphs are also reflected in empirical results with the training algorithms, both the (full-loss / quadratic-time) version and the (sampled-loss / stochastic / scalable) version. In the paper, we focus on the quadratic version since we are more interested in the capacities of the different models, as opposed to the training algorithm (that is, we use the best possible training algorithm to approximate how well the different models possibly could be fit, without regard to scalability), and we only mention the stochastic version to show that a scalable extension is possible.

content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
The work presents a way of decomposing a symmetric adjacency matrix using a Sigmoid and two lower rank matrices representing vectors for homophilous and heterophilous communities. Reviewers feel this is an important area with growing interest, although some earlier work Generalized RDPG also exists which the authors subsequently addressed. Reviewers also liked the model, and arboricity is a good concept to use for sparseness.  The theory shows such embeddings exist for matrices of bounded arboricity. Some experiments are done although the comparisons are limited to some earlier techniques. The paper is well written and motivated.

This is interesting work focussing on the theoretical contribution. The theory is motivated by various recent prior contributions, Peysakhovich & Bottou (2021) and Chanpuriya et al. (2020). Community detection and link prediction are demonstrated for five mid-sized data sets. Analysis of results w.r.t. heterophily on real-world data sets is not done, although as the authors say, a clear definition of heterophily is not currently accepted.  Note also, link prediction methods not based on matrix factorisation can be superior and have not been compared.

Support for acceptance at ICLR was not strong. Reviewers had suggested a number of improvements for discussion and experimental work.  My impression is that the focus of the presentation should be reworked since the core is solid: perhaps trying to better define heterophily and doing some studies on the real data sets to show that working.  Also studies of different model dimensions $K_B$ and $k_C$ could be demonstrated since they are never known in advance.  You have some informed comments here in the response.  Setting these using ground truth would not accepted by typical experimentalists.
content.justification_for_why_not_higher_score: The paper has a good solid core, a nice model and a good theory.  Many issues and questions remain, though in experimental work, elucidating what heterophily is and really highlighting how the algorithm helps the community.
content.summary_of_AC-reviewer_meeting:
The reviewers better explained their position:  lack of modern comparisons, proper work, and the fact that it is an important problem. 
The authors Theorem 4.2 is the main contribution.
The reviewers had addressed a number of issues but yet questions about experimental work remained.
Reviewer who bought up Generalized RDPG work felt they didn't do a good enough job of addressing it in their revised paper.
For link prediction, GNNs seem to be way ahead now of matrix factorisation methods, which makes the interest in these approaches less.
